content.title: Interview: Where's Blackout 2? Treyarch, Raven Software Reveal Why We're Getting Black Ops Royale Instead
content.text: Published Mar 12, 2026, 10:00 AM EDT Call of Duty: Black Ops 4 marked the Call of Duty franchise's first foray into the Battle Royale genre. Titled Blackout, the mode skewed more heavily towards traditional BR tropes than its successor, Call of Duty: WarzoneWarzone ultimately went on to be a juggernaut, eclipsing the success of Blackout and serving as Call of Duty's sole Battle Royale experience since 2020.Despite this, fans have grown nostalgic for Blackout. Raven Software and Treyarch have heard those cries, answering them with Black Ops Royale, a new mode for Warzone that pulls heavily from Blackout for inspiration. We were able to sit down with Yale Miller, Senior Director of Production at Treyarch, and Pete Actipis, Game Director at Raven Software, to discuss how Black Ops Royale came to be and why not make a Blackout 2 instead. Related Call of Duty: Black Ops 7, Warzone Season 1 Poised to be the Largest Call of Duty Season Ever Treyarch and Raven Software have revealed what's all coming in Call of Duty: Black Ops 7 and Call of Duty: Warzone Season 1, and it's a lot. [Hardcore Gamer] We first got word of Black Ops Royale at Call of Duty Next last year. At the time, it was introduced as a Blackout-inspired mode. Now we know what it is. In your words, what is Black Ops Royale to you? What do you want players to know about the mode going in? [Pete Actipis]Black Ops Royale is a Call of Duty Warzone battle royale game that's stripped down to the core mechanics of looting, scavenging, and being scrappy. Nothing is guaranteed. It's a game that takes Black Ops DNA to heart and Blackout as a mode, as inspiration. It's about teamwork. It's about discoverability. It's about building your strength over the course of a match. [Yale Miller] I think, for me, it's just a legitimate kind of a new take on the core fundamentals of BR and Warzone. It's respecting the DNA from before by taking inspiration from Blackout. It's about having something that feels like a new way to play, not just a tweak on a mode. There's a lot of nostalgia for Blackout, especially now that Warzone has felt stagnant for a while. Where do you believe this nostalgia has come from and why do you think Warzone has stagnated? Why not make a Blackout 2 instead of working within the confines of Warzone? [Pete Actipis] Well, we wanted to create a new experience for Warzone. So, we don't really feel confined with this mode. Instead, we wanted to try and break the barriers. There are some systems in Warzone which just work well, and so it's like, why reinvent something that maybe doesn't need to be reinvented? Recreating Blackout wasn't our goal. It was about taking the things that worked well in Blackout and creating a new experience from the ground up that is more pure battle royale at its core, but done in a Warzone way. This is meant to stand alongside Battle Royale and Resurgence. We didn't want to cut any corners and we wanted this to have the systems and mechanics and map and space that made sense to make this mode shine. [Yale Miller] We talk about it a bunch. Blackout was 2018. It was a long time ago, right? There's a lot of things in Blackout that, when we started like thinking working on this with Raven, thought there's no way we would do that again. If we were just remaking the thing, we'd be stuck with some things that frankly are, you know, outdated. Blackout is not the mode that we would make today. It's just like, MP, we're not going to recreate MP from BO4 or BO2, we're going to look at what can we do better? Move the ball forward. You talked about going back to the core roots of Battle Royale. Infinity Ward tried that back in 2022 with Warzone 2.0 and it didn't go so well. There was quite a bit of backlash to the removal of loadouts and Perks, the changes to movement and alterations to the Gulag. What steps are you taking to ensure people this is still Warzone, but fresh enough to ward off stagnation? [Pete Actipis] We have to take some risks, right? That's kind of what we're doing with this mode. We know that players love playing with their guns, right? At the same time, there's a learning curve about what weapons and attachments are good. There's a cognitive load that's inherent to Warzone right now, and so we wanted to take a fresh take on how you acquire weapons, and upgrade weapons. It's different, and we're asking players to go on a journey with us, but we really feel like we've created these new systems that still respect player agency. It is different than loadouts, but we're hoping that at the end of each match you feel as powerful or even more powerful in a different way. It's a different sort of flavor. The whole mode itself requires a different strategy than what you normally have been grinding for the last six years in BR. [Yale Miller] It's part of getting back to the roots where you boot in, drop in, and that's all you need to do. From there, the match takes you on a journey and how you choose to go is going to impact where you go. You don't need to do a bunch of setup in the beginning. No hunting for money or worrying about planning your loadout. It's just go in and play. The other thing is that Warzone is big and we're not going to stop offering different ways to play? Regular, traditional Warzone BR is still going to be there. Resurgence is still going to be there. This is about giving something different to players. There are going to be players who are going to think this is great and love. Others won't, but the other modes are still going to be there. I think with Warzone 2.0, it was a different thing where the experience people enjoyed was gone. Black Ops Royale isn't replacing the other modes. The lack of loadouts really helped with variety. Players don't have direct access to meta weapons and gear. An interesting thing you're doing with Black Ops Royale is upgrade paths where the attachments are pre-defined based on a weapon's archetype. What was the thinking behind upgrade paths vs. Blackout's open system? [Yale Miller] We talked about this one a bunch. It came down to that, when people think about it they don't actually remember the difficulty sorting through attachments. Wrong one, wrong one, wrong one, wrong one, wrong one, wrong one, wrong one. Oh, I got the thing. There's attachment, run over. Oh, it's not, it's the wrong one. You know, a lot of issues like that. Instead now, it's you've got a gun, and you can quickly figure out its upgrade path. You just know the gun's going to get better. [Pete Actipis] Yeah, this almost feels it's, you know, it's I don't want to say a better mousetrap. It's a different mousetrap because it's all about making players feel like they're getting stronger. [Yale Miller] We want you to be excited when you see one of these tokens. Not excited, then you run up and go, oh, it's the wrong one. [Pete Actipis] There's still a lot of skill required, like Yael's saying, but like we felt that there was a different way to tackle the problem while still paying off the feeling that you got in Blackout, which is that sense of growth over the course of the match. We wanted you in the fight quicker, and not stuck trying to figure out which attachment do I want. [Yale Miller] I died many times in Blackout while staring at my loadout and figuring out which attachments to drop or not. We unanimously wanted to try something that was more straightforward where you just got better. We knew we needed to have a system where the weapons got better. [Pete Actipis] It really is a sum of the parts, right? I don't think this system would work as well from what we've seen if you only had half of the components in there, right? It's a harmony between weapon acquisition, weapon growth, and how the weapon performs, because we wanted them to be meaty and meaningful step changes between rarities. Black Ops Royale is solving a major issue that has permeated FPS titles: laser-beam weapons. You're introducing significant bullet drop that requires players to think about distance before committing to a firefight. What led to the implementation of this mechanic? If successful, could we see it make its way into Battle Royale, Resurgence and maybe even multiplayer? [Pete Actipis] That was a key mechanic in Blackout, so, when we were talking about what needs to come over, it was clear that weapon handling was something we had to bring back. Whether or not it permeates to other modes in Warzone, we'll see. We'll see how players adopt and like it. [Yale Miller] Same thing on the MP side. We've talked about it, but the distances in MP don't matter as much. I don't see it happening for BO7, but I think we're excited to see what the data says. Black Ops Royale is available March 12 at 9pm PT as part of a free update for Call of Duty: Warzone. Be sure to read our preview of it here.
